utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies, of course. Mr. Stamp, you were re-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Golubovic. Yesterday in answer to some questions you said that certain documents you were shown indicate that the Minister Stojiljkovic had appointed one Petric to be chief of the Pristina SUP; Janijicevic to be chief of the SUP Kosovska Mitrovica; and another Gavranic, another person by the name of Gavranic to be chief of the SUP in Gnjilane. Do you know to whom these SUP chiefs in Kosovo reported up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they reported to, probably to the staff; however, not only they but the others too, the existing chiefs of secretariats reported to the ministry in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if I understand your answer. You're saying that they probably reported to the staff and then you go on to say that the existing chiefs reported to the ministry in Belgrade or is that you do not know to who they reported?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the existing organisational structure. All the chiefs reported to the chief of the public security and the minister. As the minister appointed them, they reported to the minister; but as they were working in Kosovo, they most probably reported or were assigned certain tasks and responsibilities. Depending on the territory in which they were active, they reported to the staff in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The format or the means in which they -- by which they reported to the chief of the public security?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For those in Kosovo, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up the document that was used yesterday, it has the number D0020357, and it is the rules on the internal organisation of the Ministry of Interior. If we could go to Article 13 thereof, and if we could do that in the B/C/S version as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it on the monitor, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page. The article starts by reading -- by going: "The following organisational units shall be established at the Ministry headquarters ..." And if we could move to the next page in B/C/S, you will see them listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They are referred to as administrations. Did these administrations have heads or chiefs of administration?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. Heading each administration there was a leader, a chief, a head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in terms of the organisational structure of the public service or the public security department, how did they -- or where did the chiefs of these administrations stand in relation to the chief of the RJB?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were subordinated to him. The chief of the department was in charge of all those administrations; and therefore, he was superior to all those chiefs. When talking about the administration for crime prevention or the administration for traffic police, they were in that respect independent when working in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Article 14 deals with the responsibilities of the crime prevention administration. Who in 1999 was the head of the crime prevention administration?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Ilic was the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's General Dragan Ilic?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to Article 15. It deals with the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the police administration in 1999?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I know that there was some changes there. Now I'm not sure whether it was Obrad Stevanovic or General Simic. I can't be quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Obrad Stefanovic was also an assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but for a while he was also a head of the police administration. And General Simic was also appointed to that position for a while in 1999, but I can't be quite certain --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The police administration also had responsibilities for the special police units; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- I don't know about the special units, but for separate police units, the logistics, the preparations within the framework of the plan of national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. If you could look at the end of Article 15, five paragraphs up from the end of Article 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see it says here that: "The Administration shall comprise: The Police Department, the Department For Public Law and Order, the Department for Special Police Units and the Reserve ..." Do you recall that being the situation in 1999?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as there were special police units within the framework of the secretariat. That is probably what the situation was in 1999 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look quickly at Article 17, that's operation centre. I don't know if we need to go to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But can I ask you: Do you recall who was the head of the operations centre in the RJB in 1999?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I know who was in charge before that, but for 1999 I don't know. I can't remember. Because as chief of the secretariat and other chiefs of secretariats, only exceptionally did we have contact with them. They were special units according to this organisational structure so that the operations centre is something I don't know who was in charge of. I know before that it was General Trujic [phoen], but as for 1999 I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Article 18 deals with the border police administration. I just want to ask you, since you have been asked some questions about the border police and your SUP covered areas that bordered Romania, do you know who the head of the border police administration was in 1999?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name. These people changed quite frequently. I cannot give you a definite answer because the personnel changed. Maybe you can assist me and then I can perhaps recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember if it's General Petar Dojkovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. The name is not familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's not in order to remind the witness. The witness said that he can't remember and that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Actually, I -- the witness asked to be reminded, and I -- I misread a signal from my friend. I thought the name of who was the head of that department in 1999 was not in issue, was not a matter in which there was challenge if I put it to the witness, but I see that I misread the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, what's been done has been done. Carry on now, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Finally in this regard, Witness, Articles 23 and 24 deals with the administrations for joint affairs of the ministry and board and lodgings administration. Do you recall who was the head of that -- of those two administrations.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Heading the -- that administration, I think it was General Zekovic, for joint affairs, and this included lodgings and other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he also an assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all these heads of administrations had the rank of assistant ministers. I'm not familiar with the decisions appointing them, but I assume that that is the rank they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I asked you a question yesterday, and I'm not sure if we got a clear answer. Can I ask you this question in respect to the relationship between Mr. Djordjevic and Mr. Stojiljkovic: Do you know of any situation in which Mr. Djordjevic did not obey an order given to him by Mr. Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I wasn't present there to be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Stojiljkovic? Is he alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He committed suicide in 2001 or 2002, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I don't think I have anything -- well, before I do that, may I just -- nothing further for the witness, Your Honour. I'm reminded there always being something I forgot that I should seek leave to tender the laws -- the law of -- yes, it was used yesterday by Defence and Your Honour had indicated that they were interested in 1 to 10. I think having regard to the indictment which names certain people as members of the JCE, some of whose names he has called in relation to some of these areas I've asked about -- I think the remaining sections, about 30, should go in. But in the circumstances I think it probably would be more practical if the entire document went in as I believe as other witnesses come to testify in the course of this case reference will be made to various parts of the document. I did discuss it with the Defence, and I don't think they object to the whole document going in although, of course, I understand, Your Honours, would only be interested at least for the time being in what the witness has commented about. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will then receive the whole of the document. Is it to be a Defence or a Prosecution exhibit? Have you resolved that between you, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm afraid that -- that issue escaped us. It could be a Prosecution exhibit. I don't think it matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, as you're on your feet, it will be a Prosecution exhibit, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00357, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may be able to assist us further, Mr. Golubovic, about the events of the 5th, 6th, and 7th of April because we're not entirely clear about some matters. The truck, as you'd understand it, had been found in the river on the 5th of April, 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the information I had. I wasn't there on the 5th or the 4th or the 6th until the evening, so that is the information that I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you first heard about it at about 6.30 in the evening of the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: By that time, as you understood it, the truck had been partly eased out of the water, the refrigerated part opened, and it had been seen that there were some bodies in the truck?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the information I received. The refrigerator truck was hauled out around midday, the gates were opened. When they saw the bodies, they closed the gates immediately. And the investigating judge and the prosecutor left the scene, and the police just secured the refrigerator truck physically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think you said that it had been estimated at that time there was some 20 or 30 bodies in the truck. That's what you were told --

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And these were thought to be Albanian?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the initial viewing and the information later, so when they were seen, it was thought that they were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I think you mentioned that was in part because of the clothing that were on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly on the basis of the clothing; and secondly, on the basis of the inscription on the truck which was visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was from a town in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it was not until the next day that you learnt, I gather, that in fact there were many more bodies than 20 or 30?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the next day. One could say it was the next day, but it was during the night after a certain period of time, maybe it was 11.00 or 12.00, that is, midnight, and then in the early morning. And even then the exact number could not be established. As far as I know and as I was told, the exact number was established on the 7th when those bodies were moved from the refrigerator truck to another truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were these male bodies?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that there were men and women, not just male but also female bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And they were in what might be called Albanian clothing; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who saw them, that is what they concluded, mainly on the basis of the clothing worn by women because they aware "dimijas" as we call them, even though those kind of pantaloons are worn by Romanis and Serbs as well down there in the south but that was one of the indicators pointing to the fact that they were Albanians, even though such clothing is worn by gypsies as well and also elderly Serb women living in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were there any children, any bodies of children?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was mention of one or more children, anyway, younger people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Originally you thought from what you were told or originally others had thought this was a traffic accident; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was what I was told at the time, that that was what they had thought the previous day. Sometime the previous day, prior to the 5th, something to the effect that there had been a traffic accident, because the road in that area skirts the river Danube. There was a dangerous bend in that road where traffic accidents were frequent. The vehicles involved would skid off the road and down into the river and that's where they were looking for it. That was probably the reason that led them to believe there had been a traffic accident and that the refrigerator truck had simply slid off the road and down into the river. Later on I was able to draw my own inference. I was told that on that day the chief over in Kladovo, I think, had made sure that there were a number of trucks on their way to help with the bodies that were there as a result of that traffic accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What of the driver of the truck? What did you learn about him?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they said that there was a diver who inspected the area and that the driver was not found because one the refrigerator truck had been hauled out of the water there was no driver in the cabin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The road where this occurred skirting along the edge of the Danube, is that a road that would normally be used travelling from the area of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, rarely if ever. Probably while the relations were different it was still being used for bringing supplies into the area or from that area into Kosovo, maybe it was used for that purpose. The road was much used by Romanians as well crossing the Djerdap. It was used for travelling and for trade purposes not only by people from that area but also from other areas, such as Belgrade, Kosovo, Montenegro, and so on and so forth, this being the shortest route between the south of Serbia and Romania. There is a border crossing called Centralija that was a border crossing to Romania, and the same thing applied the other way around from Romania into Serbia. At the time it was a much travelled area. It was also the shortest route connecting Romania and Bulgaria. Nearby, Negotin is another border crossing, the one to Bulgaria. Therefore, this was Europe's shortest route across Romania on to Bulgaria and then on to Greece and Turkey. Therefore, it was a road that was frequently used by everyone, not only the people who lived locally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It wasn't, though, the normal road from Kosovo to, say, Belgrade, was it?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't marked that way on the maps. It wasn't marked as a convenient route to Europe either, not specifically. One had to take various roads in order to reach this one. There is one across Pozarevac through Velika Gradiska and then straight onto Kladovo. There is another route that joins up with this one the one from Bor, Zajecar-Bor-Nis, and so on and so forth. There is a whole network of roads there channelling many of these routes into the single one that led on further south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I understand from your evidence you were told that when the refrigerator truck door was opened and bodies were found, that the public prosecutor and the investigating judge were there at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that's what I was told. As soon as it was opened, I realised there were bodies inside so the door was shut. The public prosecutor and the investigating judge were there. They saw this too. The door was shut, and they stopped the on-site investigation that had been in progress. You must have seen photographs of that refrigerator truck that had been hauled out partly from the Danube the previous day. The Kladovo department forensic technician probably took photographs, and then they put a stop to this on-site investigation, once the judicial officials had stopped it. So this was an end of the cooperation between the police and the judicial organs. All that remains are the recorded images. I saw some of those in the media and the press and I saw some of those during the Milosevic trial here, but all of this was done before the on-site investigation was terminated. And that was done as soon as they had realised that there were bodies involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So I take it then that the public prosecutor and the investigating judge were there to look into what was thought to be a traffic accident of a truck entering the river?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't know themselves until the refrigerator truck was opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The presence of the bodies, from what you have said, made this a responsibility of the district prosecutor and the district investigating judge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under the Law on Criminal Procedure of Serbia, this would have been the case. The district court has powers up to a certain level. This can be expressed in monetary terms, too, up to a certain value, and then there is a range of sentences in these cases it would have been a smaller sentence and this would have been something for the district bodies or municipal bodies to deal with. When larger numbers are involved or more serious accidents, then it would have been up to the district prosecutor and the district court because the sentences imposed in cases such as these are, as a rule, more severe or higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mentioned that they had been notified after the bodies were found. Do you know who did that, who notified them?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you mean the district prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The district prosecutor and the district investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was normal procedure for them to be informed by the municipal bodies, although, based on what I was told at the time, they had been informed by the municipal prosecutor and the municipal investigating judge, in addition to which they had been informed by whichever unit of the Ministry of Internal Affairs happened to be on duty at the time. So they were informed through two different channels, the municipal, judicial channels, and the police - and when I say the police I mean the Kladovo police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you aware that either the district prosecutor or the district investigating judge attended at the scene?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. When I was there they never showed up, and I don't think they showed up the next day either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, you telephoned General Djordjevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you told him what had been reported to you at that stage?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that was the first telephone conversation you had with him?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was it during this conversation that he said he would ring you back in 10 or 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When he rang you back, can you tell us what it was that he said?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, he told me that we should bury the bodies. The number being bandied about was still between 20 and 30. He said we should bury those, that this was an order from the minister. That was the basic thing that was said and the conclusion that I drew based on that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did he say where they were to be buried?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Kladovo most probably. We were in Kladovo so that was the implication, that we should deal with it in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you arranged then with -- I think you said it was Vukasin Sperlic - for the removal and burial of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in his office. I wasn't the only person present nor was he. There were other people who were there, such as the prosecutor and the investigating judge. They were also there. They left the office at one point but there must have been five or six of us there in the office. We received this order and we started discussing how we should go about this, how we should carry out the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And this would have been somewhere between 9.00 and 10.00 at night on the 6th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about 9.00 I think. The conversation took place just before 9.00, so it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And where were the bodies to be buried?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not particularly familiar with the area, but there were different proposals, one of those being the local cemetery, but the local cemetery was not big enough to hold those bodies. Then someone came up with a different location, I don't remember who proposed what precisely but there were several proposals, and then we tried to narrow this down in order to find the best place to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And this had to be done while it was still dark I gather because of your concern at --

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- bombing and the Romanians?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during that night. I do apologise, but I have to say this again. This is on the Danube and the border is down the middle of the Danube between Serbia and Romania; on the other side of the border is Orsava, a place in Romania, hosting a unit of Romania's fleet, a unit of their military. This is an open area with a clear line of sight. It is easy to see both riverbanks from that area. This was an open area, so that was one of the reasons this was done that night under the cover of the dark so to speak, and NATO planes were flying overhead not dropping any bombs at the time, but we could hear them fly overhead. That was the situation. This had to be done at night and not by daylight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, how long did you stay there that night, the 6th of April, on the morning of the 7th? Are you able to say when you left?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left with Toma Miladinovic. I drove a car as well because my driver had taken off previously to take the refrigerator truck back to Belgrade and I know I was at work sometime past 7.00. It takes about one hour to reach Bor from Kladovo, perhaps even over an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You spoke to General Djordjevic 9.00 or later in the evening, 9.00 or later. When was it that you left there?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left Kladovo sometime when those who were in charge of getting blankets and everything else as well as a new truck got there. Once they got in touch with us to say that all these items had been secured, we left, each in our own vehicles and with our own tasks. This may have been sometime around half past 9.00 or 10.00, maybe between 10.00 and 11.00. It wasn't much later, not much later after the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you, in effect, left the area, leaving the task of burying the bodies in the hands of the people that you had designated to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We left Kladovo, those people and I and all those of us who were present went to a place near the refrigerator truck. It wasn't that I left. Nothing was done until we got to Tekija and Tekija is the place where the refrigerator truck was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And can you say when you reached Tekija?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, as soon as we left Kladovo, about 10.00 that evening. The distance to Kladovo is 12 kilometres. If you drive there, it takes about 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it was when you were at Tekija that it became apparent that you wouldn't be able to remove all the bodies from the truck that night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when they first opened the refrigerator truck and started preparing to pull the bodies out of the truck and take them to another truck that was waiting on the road, they realised that this could hardly be done the same night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You spoke to the -- General Djordjevic again that night by telephone?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to him three or four times from Tekija that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that's when in the course of those conversations you made it clear to him that it wasn't possible to remove all the bodies that night and bury them?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was already the morning of the 7th, early morning. By this time about 30 bodies had been carried across; that's what our information indicated. It was clear that there was an even greater number of bodies still within the refrigerator truck. I got in touch with General Djordjevic; we talked. I told him that we couldn't do this. We didn't have a forensic pathologist, for example, who was present on the scene in order to carry out post mortems or attempt an identification or indeed attempt to establish the cause of death. I made it clear we couldn't finish the job that night. After some time General Djordjevic accepted this, and we stopped short of finishing the job. It was already morning by this time. I don't know when exactly the truck left, but it must have been about 5.00 a.m., a bit later or a bit earlier, but it was about 5.00 a.m. the truck left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which -- is this a truck that you had secured from Kladovo?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And who was driving that truck?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The driver from the original company that we got the truck from was not there; therefore, my own driver who had driven me to Kladovo, Ljubinko Stojanovic [as interpreted], drove it. I didn't quite order him, but I asked him if he would be willing to drive the truck and he said yes. He said yes and then he drove the truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it during that night you didn't have either the municipal or the district prosecutor or investigating judge at Tekija?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you didn't have any forensic assistance?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. That was the reason we wanted to take the bodies somewhere where they could be examined by a pathologist, not just one but a team of pathologists; and that meant Nis or Belgrade because down in the area covered by the secretariat there wasn't a single pathologist available to us or indeed any other type of forensic assistance. Even if we had buried the bodies right there, we would have had to do so most probably without first processing the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you were at Kladovo before you drove to Tekija you understood there was some 20 or 30 bodies in the truck?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That was the information I had, and the information came from the people who had opened the door during that day, had a look, and saw what they saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why did you set about organising for the burial of those bodies that night at Kladovo?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't say we actually started the burial. All we did over in Kladovo was secured some blankets that we might then use to carry the bodies over from the refrigerator truck to the truck that was waiting on the road. Nothing else was done in Kladovo and no other actions were initiated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But you discussed where they would be buried?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were discussing, there were several of us there, seven or eight people present. The people from Kladovo were supposed to secure the scene and make all these things available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I -- what I'm not clear about then is why, if you had no pathologist and no judge, either municipal or district, and no prosecutor, you would have thought of burying these bodies that night?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason was we had to move the refrigerator truck further off the road, because the people who were near the refrigerator truck said that there was already a stench spreading of decomposing bodies. It couldn't just stay like that without being dealt with, so that was the reason for us trying to deal with this as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that's why you would have moved bodies from the truck to another truck; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the refrigerator truck could no longer be operated or used. It had partly been pulled out of the river and it couldn't be started, the engine couldn't be started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But having moved the trucks from the refrigerator truck to the other truck, why would you then think to immediately bury them that night?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we first started work, it was said that we should bury the bodies that night. I told you about the minister's order that was mentioned in that conversation, and the order that we should do just that - I'm talking about the first conversation from Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You knew there were not the normal judicial and court authorities, and you knew there was not a pathologist and you were confronted with some 20 or 30 bodies in a refrigerator truck. The idea that you would simply bury them is something that I'm not able to understand as being a correct procedure to be followed.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the conditions were that prevailed at the time. There was a state of war. Most probably in a situation like that there would have been no other solutions. We didn't have the time to wait for the proper procedure to be initiated for another day or two until the bodies were secured. There were all these reasons which meant we had to do it straight away. When we saw that, we insisted -- rather, I insisted through General Djordjevic that this should be done elsewhere with due professional and forensic care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You had managed -- or those doing the work had managed to transfer some 30 bodies from the refrigerator truck to the truck you'd got there from Kladovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that was the truck then that drove that night to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem you had then was that there were many more bodies than just 20 or 30?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you couldn't find another truck that evening; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were none to go around because all the trucks owned by all the local companies had been mobilised by the army and Territorial Defence. Therefore, I asked General Djordjevic for a truck from the ministry to be dispatched to the area so that we could transport the remaining bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the -- General Djordjevic said it was an order from the minister that you should bury the bodies in Kladovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because after I had called him then some 15 or 20 minutes later he called back and that is what he said, when he called me from Belgrade in Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement you made Exhibit P352 at its end said: "I do not know if General Djordjevic consulted the minister of the interior, who was then Vlajko Stojiljkovic, or if he consulted or informed anyone else of the event concerning the refrigerator lorry before issuing his instructions to me."

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed, because he said he would call back later, that he needed to consult someone, most probably, or to inform someone about the event I had informed him about, as he was surprised hearing this from me, I could hear that by the tone of his voice, that it was with surprise that he received the news. And later on when he called, he said that it was an order from the minister. So I assumed that he had consulted the minister because if he had made the decision then he would have probably told me straight away what to do. I wouldn't have had to wait 15 or 20 minutes to wait for him to tell me what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why then did you say that you did not know if he'd consulted the minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know because I wasn't present there, but when he told me what to do after a certain period of time he said that that was the order of the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A couple of concerns about this aspect. In the statement, you make no mention of General Djordjevic saying it was an order from the minister, and yet in your yesterday here you say that's what the general told you. Can you offer an explanation why you didn't mention that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I did mention it, Your Honour. Now, whether it was in the Milutinovic trial or the Milosevic trial, maybe not quite so explicitly that the minister had ordered it but that the minister had said that that is what we should do; and I had assumed he had consulted the minister. I did say that somewhere. Maybe whoever compiled that statement, I didn't pay attention, and maybe that is why I didn't notice it; but in one of my testimonies I couldn't have said anything else because that is the truth. Now, in what form I expressed that is another matter. It was customary for us to refer to someone when something needs to be done, someone higher up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was said in your statement is that: "Colonel-General Djordjevic phoned me back some 10 to 15 minutes later and instructed me that the bodies, which at that stage we believed numbered around 30 were to be removed from the refrigerator truck and buried in the area of Kladovo in the course of the night." Now, there's no suggestion there that he was conveying to you the order of the minister.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly whoever was compiling the statement didn't ask me that at the time. Whoever wrote the statement didn't ask me that question. I did sign the statement. Maybe he didn't think it was important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But it was very clear to you, was it, that the general had said that this was an order from the minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he said something to that effect at the end of that conversation while I was in Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You accepted that as correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did accept it because my superior told me that, and he gave me the order as to what I should do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that brings me back then to the question why you said expressly: "I do not know if General Djordjevic consulted the minister of the interior ..."

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that because they were always next to one another in the same place in Belgrade during the war. The headquarters where they were then, I think it was in Majke Jevrosime Street. That is where the office of the minister and of General Djordjevic were situated and some other officers because they were not in the building of the ministry. These were reserve wartime positions that they took up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you see, that tends to explain how he could have consulted the minister. What you're saying, you accepted that he did consult the minister and was conveying to you the minister's order; and yet you say expressly: "I do not know if General Djordjevic consulted the minister ..." Can you see the difficulty that I'm looking at?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I said I don't know because I wasn't there, who -- I didn't know who he consulted. So I assumed, so it's my assumption, that he consulted the minister because he told me to wait and he would call back. So he must have consulted someone and reached some agreement with someone. And the conclusion I drew, in view of the fact that under those circumstances he was probably close to the minister. Now, whether he called him up by phone, but I assumed he consulted the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The understanding I have from what you've said is that you were quite satisfied that it was the order of the minister when the general told you that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accepted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if you accepted that, wouldn't you have said in your statement that he had consulted the minister before giving you instructions?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that I did say this in my testimony, that he had consulted someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he had consulted someone, does that mean that you were not clear whether he consulted the minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I wasn't present there so I don't know who he consulted, but I assumed that it was the minister. I didn't hear it or see it, and that is why I assumed it and that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I can remind you of the full sentence, I read it to you earlier: "I do not know if General Djordjevic consulted the minister of the interior, who was then Vlajko Stojiljkovic, or if he consulted or informed anyone else of the event concerning the refrigerator lorry before issuing his instructions to me." So are you now saying that you were satisfied that he had spoken to the minister?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I drew the conclusion that most probably he did. What I said is quite correct. That is my statement. I think he consulted someone, I don't know who, because I was not there to see it, and I assumed that it was with the minister. He could have consulted someone else. This was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When -- what he told you is that he was giving you the order of the minister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he rang up in Kladovo during our second conversation, his first call-up from Belgrade, the first time he called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it was the minister's order and not his order?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to that effect, but he passed it on to me, so I don't know how to explain this. He passed on this to me and he referred to the minister. He said that the minister had said this just in the same way that I told the others who were present there that general had said such and such a thing. So I also referred to him, to General Djordjevic when we were discussing what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you gave your evidence in Milutinovic, I think your express reference was that he would -- he told me: "To stay in my office until after he'd consulted the minister or somebody else; and then he said that he'd be calling me back with further instructions." Is that something that was said to you?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gave several statements, and I testified here twice. I cannot use the same words each time and repeat what I said the first time and the second, but in substance that is the truth. Now, whether I put it in this way or in another way, in view of the situation I was in at the time I may have said something else or my understanding may have been different. But the substance of it is that the conversation flowed in that way. The conversation didn't end in one minute or two, it must have lasted five or six minutes, maybe longer, both of these conversations; and then different words are used which may be interpreted in a different way in one situation than in another. So so I had the same thing in mind and I said the same thing, but if I didn't use the same words then that's another matter. Even now I don't think I can repeat the same words that I used in my statements and in testifying in Milosevic or in the other trial; but the gist of it is the same, maybe not in the same words. In 1999, the words may have been different but the substance is the same. So I cannot confirm each and every word used, especially not now, ten years later. I don't know, Your Honour, whether you have understood my explanation, but the gist of it is that I'm telling the truth but maybe in different words then and in different words now and different words may be used in the different statements but the substance is there. If anyone present could confirm this, they may remember what I said because I wasn't alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll leave the exact words alone, but can you tell us whether General Djordjevic mentioned the minister when you first spoke to him and before he hung up, telling you to wait until he called back or whether the general mentioned the minister when he rang back?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he rang back, not the first time -- neither did I mention the minister nor did he, that is when I called him up from Kladovo, the minister was not mentioned. But during the conversation that we had when he called back, this was mentioned. The function of the minister, that is quite certain. Now, whether I interpreted that correctly, but the minister as such was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And this was after General Djordjevic rang you back when you were still at Kladovo?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in this second conversation, or rather, the first time he actually called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And he gave you to understand then that he was giving you the minister's order?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That passage I've read to you twice from your statement concludes by you saying of General Djordjevic "... I don't know if he consulted or informed anyone else before issuing his instructions to me." Now, "his" is General Djordjevic, it's not the minister. Is there some simple explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stated and I'm stating once again, I couldn't know who General Djordjevic consulted in Belgrade, but in view of the fact that I waited for him to call back, I drew the conclusion that he had consulted someone. And from the conversation we had during this second conversation, the minister was mentioned, and that was the conclusion I made. He may have consulted someone else or several people, I don't know that, and that is why I said that I only assume that he had consulted the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think we have gone over that very carefully and got your full explanations now. You did also say that when you spoke to the general during the night of the 6th and the morning of the 7th in one of the conversations he gave you some instructions about the refrigerated truck. What did he want done with that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted the refrigerator truck to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that done?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done several days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how was that done?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the refrigerator truck was transferred from Tekija to Kladovo to the work organisation Komunalac, the public utility company and that it was there for a day or two. And after that it was driven to Petrovo Selo, set alight, and as it couldn't be destroyed like that, then explosives were used to destroy it. So this was several days after Kladovo, after Tekija. Because when I went to Bor, I had no further contact nor did I inquire nor did anyone call me in connection with the destruction of that truck. It was agreed that night in Tekija, and it was left to the people in Kladovo to do it. Now, exactly what happened -- but my information is that it spent about two days in that company and that afterwards it was transferred to Petrovo Selo and destroyed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you understand why the general wanted the truck destroyed?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can only be an assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're saying he didn't tell you?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me to destroy it, but why, I could only speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you left instructions then for that to be done; is that it?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was taken to Kladovo, it spent some time there, and after conditions were -- made it possible, it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You left those instructions without any other special directions about the truck?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Simply, in general terms, that it should be destroyed. Whether it should be set alight or blown up, I'm not an expert for these things, I didn't know. I just told my subordinates that they should do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This was a truck in which some perhaps 80 bodies had been found. Wasn't that something that ought to have been the subject of official investigation by the examining -- by the prosecutor and the examining judge?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably that should have been done had the situation been normal and normal conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djurdjic, and Mr. Stamp, there have been some matters as you've heard that have not been clear to the Chamber. In view of the matters we've asked, we would invite, first you, Mr. Djurdjic, if there's any further question you would like to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I shall try to clear up even further, if possible, though you've done that perfectly well, a couple of brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Golubovic, am I right in saying that when you were informed about the truck in the river that there was no driver and that it didn't have the windshield?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I wasn't informed about all the details, but I was just informed in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right that when we are talking about the road along the Danube that because of the sanctions that had been enforced on Serbia and the FRY in 1991, and they lasted until 2001, that this road was very important for the transport of goods and that it was a busy road of goods going to all parts of Serbia and that Kosovo was also supplied with goods from Romania and Bulgaria along that route?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was used, that vehicles drove along that route, not only from Serbia but also most probably from Montenegro, from Kosovo, from Romania, Bulgaria, et cetera. So it was frequently used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And am I also right in saying that you personally were not present and you didn't hear Minister Stojiljkovic tell General Djordjevic what he passed on to you, and that is why the statement you gave was in the way it was?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I told Their Honours. I wasn't present, I don't know who he consulted, but I assume that in view of the time that elapsed until he called me back that he had consulted someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Earlier you were asked about the name of the driver of the truck and that's at page 18, line 24 and the record indicates that you said that the driver of the first truck, that is, your driver that you sent with the truck with the bodies to Belgrade is Stojanovic, which I don't think is what I heard. So could you just please repeat the name of the driver of the truck.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubinko Ursuljanovic, not Stojanovic, you can find that in my statement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague and for the assistance you've been able to give over two days of evidence. We're grateful for your attempts clearly to answer the questions that have been put to you. You may now of course return to your normal activities and the -- when the court rises you will be able to leave and the court officer will assist you. So thank you indeed. It's now 5.15, which is a convenient time for the first break. We'll resume at 5.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everybody in and around the courtroom. The next witness is Mr. Radojkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please read aloud the -- what is written on the card that is given to you now, the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. I think Mr. Neuner has some questions for you. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your name is Bosko Radojkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radojkovic, you were born on the 5th of February, 1956, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And from 1974 until 2006 you worked as a policeman, namely as a crime technician?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you are retired since 2006?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to show you your statement which you have given in June 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter number 5139 on our screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise your statement and -- can you see it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is this statement complete and a true and accurate reflection of what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can only see the front page, but I do believe that that is the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, this is just the first page of a couple of pages of the statement. We have uploaded electronically is complete here. You see, for example, the second page here, the third page --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the last page, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With this witness explanation could I seek to tender 65 ter 5139 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00358, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you testified also in the Milutinovic et al case, didn't you in November 2006?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And could we have the 65 ter number 5138, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is the first page, and it's in English, of the words you've spoken in the Milutinovic case. It's a verbatim record. Do you agree that together, with the statement, this transcript truly and accurately reflects what you would say if you would give today your testimony orally here in court?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 5138 being tendered, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm reading out a summary of the witness's evidence. In 1999 Mr. Radojkovic was a policeman and senior crime technician in the Serbian Ministry of Interior in the Kladovo police station in Serbia. On 4 April 1999 the witness was called to the Danube river at Tekija in Serbia. In the Danube a refrigerator truck had been found. The witness took a number of photographs. In the following days, the witness assisted in the recovery of the lorry from the river and examined the contents of the truck. It contained bodies which were loaded on to other trucks which left towards Donji Milanovac in north-western direction. Following instructions from his superior, the witness later disposed of the truck and blew it up with explosives. The witness was interviewed about the refrigerator truck incident by a ministerial working group formed by the MUP in 2001. On 26th June that year the working group delivered an official communique outlining the result of their inquiries. Part of the communique related to the work of this witness. The witness also participated in exhumations in Petrovo Selo in the spring and summer of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now a couple of documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I'm looking at the summary that I received and the last two sentences read out by my learned friend, Mr. Neuner, are simply not there -- or at least -- I may have misunderstood. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yeah, I didn't read out the summary word by word, but I shortened it even in certain instances. The witness also had mentioned Petrovo Selo in his statement which I tendered a moment ago. So I would proceed with Your Honour's leave to the first document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 1.01, a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And, Witness, I would ask you with the assistance of the usher to mark us some place names here on the map. Firstly I would ask you to encircle Kladovo where your police station was.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark a 1 next to the encirclement.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next encircle please mark where Bor is.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mark a 2 next to this, please.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the next location, please, Tekija itself where the truck was found.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Please mark a 3.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. What roughly is the distance between Tekija and Prizren in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think about 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Then I would ask you to mark Donji Milanovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And while the witness is doing this, this place is mentioned twice in the Milutinovic transcript which was just tendered by this witness on transcript pages 7449 and 7452 for Your Honours' reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you mark a number 4 next to Donji Milanovac.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Then, please, Belgrade and circle Belgrade and mark a number 5.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but I don't see why we would have this witness mark Belgrade. Where can I find a reference for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have no idea, Mr. Djurdjic, but I think we're going to waste more time dealing with that than we are with having the witness mark Belgrade. With a bit of luck, most of us would be able to find Belgrade if we had to. Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain roughly what the difference between Tekija and Belgrade is please. The distance -- I apologise, the distance in kilometres between Tekija and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: About 270 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now mark or encircle Petrovo Selo and mark a 6 next to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: While the witness is doing this, Your Honours, this place is mentioned on page -- transcript page 7453 of the Milutinovic transcript by this witness and on page 3 of the statement which was just tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would seek to tender this annotated map as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00360, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would now like to show 65 ter 596 to this witness. We can zoom maybe in a little bit on the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what is marked here, what is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is one of the photographs that I took on the spot. This photograph was taken after the rear end of the truck, or rather, its cargo compartment had been hauled up ashore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Had the truck any licence plate when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you describe the dark part on the right door?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: What we can see on the door is a crack towards the rear or the lower part of the right-hand door on the cargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What, if anything, was protruding from the right back door?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can see a leg sticking out. This is a very poor-quality copy of the photo, but you can see the ladder up into the back of the truck and you can see a human foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you, with the assistance of the usher, mark the leg. And we have a couple of pictures coming so if he could just hold the pen for now. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is encircling the lower part of what he believes is a leg, and I would seek with that explanation to tender that exhibit which is 65 ter 596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we move to the next picture which is 65 ter 599. I think the witness has the pen now so can -- yeah, could we zoom in, please, on the front of this vehicle here in front of us, even a little bit more, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And we see here again this truck. Could you tell us -- I can read here the words "Pik Progre." What does this mean on the door?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It reads "Pik Progres, Exportna-Klanica Prizren" there's a telephone number there and a fax number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Who was operating this company in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was a state-owned company, socially owned, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you just encircle the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The usher doesn't need to come because he can just encircle it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- the "Pik Progres" part, I mean the -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And with that explanation I would seek to tender 65 ter 599.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Moving on to Exhibit 601, please. And now with the following picture I would just ask you to point out to Your Honours what the difference is between this new picture and the previous two pictures at which we looked is. You can zoom in a little bit to assist you. What are the main differences?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the rear end of the cargo compartment, the door, the crack is no longer there, the foot is no longer there. I think there were two feet sticking out as a matter of fact. That is no longer to be seen. You can see a piece of tin here that was used to cover the crack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you mark where the tin is which covered the crack. And circle it, please, and mark a 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So we don't see any crack at all?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the second -- the second difference?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think one can no longer see the inscription on the passenger door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you mark where no longer the inscriptions are on the passenger door by encircling it and mark a 2 next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then did this truck in the state in which you took a photograph here have a licence plate?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not sure if there is one in this photograph, though. At any rate, they are nowhere to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain to me why or who was involved in covering the back door with the tin and with removing the inscription of the company from Prizren from the front door?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The crack on the right-hand door of the cargo compartment was covered by me. The person who helped me was Zivadin Djordjevic, the diver who was with me; and some other people brought a tin sheet and a corkscrew as well as a pair of screws for me to be able to affix it and to be able to keep the crack from opening, from spreading. As for the inscription on the door, I was the person who painted it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With these explanations I would seek to tender the photo with the 65 ter 601.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to move on to the next exhibit, a press article, and that's 65 ter number 566.01. While it comes up I can read out to save some time the headline already of that article. "Refrigerator truck in the Danube. Bodies in the truck," it is entitled. We would need from that article in B/C/S only the right page, if you could screen in on the right page only. Yes. And if we could even enlarge on the left column, please, only the left column I need. Yes. And if we could enlarge even a little bit further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, bearing in mind the statements that I have seen, I think the witness should first be asked whether he has read the article; and if so, when. Just as a reference, I do believe that it's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that while you were here in proofing you have read this article?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do believe that I did. I read the article back when it was first published, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I hope my learned colleague is satisfied now. I'm interested in the second paragraph of the left column. I think it is -- if we could scroll down a little bit starting with this "tako." And in English it is page 2, the third-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you could just read silently to yourself this paragraph. The third-last paragraph I would only need starting with the word "finally." Yes, thank you. So mentioning is made here in the article about a location of a truck, and it says it's near to Captain Koca's monument, the truck. My question to you is: The truck with which you dealt, was this truck located near the Captain Koca monument and what is the Captain Koca monument if it was located there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Captain Koca Andjelkovic, that's who the monument is to. The distance between the axis -- the entry to Tekija all the way from Kladovo and the monument itself is about a kilometre. This was an old statue, a monument that had been submerged in the Danube at one point and a copy was made and placed there. This is simply as a reference point for the location of the truck and is referred to that way in this newspaper piece or article. So there is a monument there and the monument is to Captain Koca Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So do I take it that this journalist is also reporting about the same truck with which you also dealt in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He's trying to write about that event because that was the only event that took place near the monument to Koca Andjelkovic near Tekija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I ask that the 65 ter number 566.01 is tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the date of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The date is the - if we could zoom out a little bit - is from 1999. On the bottom of this copy which we secured this morning only I believe it says 16 September 1999. That's why we secured a now copy from a library in Novi Sad this morning. If we could even enlarge it further -- 15th of September, 1999, Your Honours. I correct myself. As far as we could see, it's the earliest point in time that the incident was reported. The incident dates back to 4/5 April 1999 as Your Honours have noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the name of the publication?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The name of the publication is -- it's also stated in the full translation. Timocka Krimi Revija. It is not translated here. Maybe I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what Timocka Krimi Revija means or could you explain? Do you know that magazine?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's a local or regional paper carrying mostly reports about crimes and certain incidents of that kind. It is published in Zajecar. A friend of mine, a colleague from the past, Vitomirovic, wrote it. I saw that article in 1999 only I forgot what it contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And did you bring that article to the attention of one of your superiors at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have anyone to inform. These are newspapers sold at kiosks, but the journalist brought it to the police station and he would always give us three or four copies free so there was no point me informing anyone about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is it a daily or a weekly newspaper?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's a monthly or fortnightly newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you said a moment ago that the journal was brought to the police station. To which police station was it brought to by the journalist?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The police station in Kladovo. The journalist and editor is a former colleague of ours. He used to work in the police and then he started working in journalism and he was always welcome. We liked to see him. I believe he took the paper to other police stations in the region for the purpose -- for publicity purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What's the name of the editor, please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Vitomirovic. He was killed in a traffic accident a couple of years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say since Mr. Vitomirovic was a former colleague that he had -- that he was well connected to police sources?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, because even this article it's just a newspaper article. The location is okay, it is correct, but the rest of it is just a journalist's story.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With this explanation could I seek that 65 ter number 566.01 --
